sources.citation: WALS Online, language Idoma (wals_code ido); StressTyp2 archive (StressTyp2-v1-archive-0415, local); PHOIBLE 2.0 language page idom1241.
sources.note: WALS has only morphosyntactic datapoints for Idoma (all from Abraham 1951), no 13A-17A prosody values; StressTyp2 has no Idoma lect (only the Ethnologue code row); PHOIBLE's sole inventory filed under idom1241 (GM 1536 'Idu') cites Blench 2010 on Idũ, a different (Plateau) language, so it is not evidence for Idoma.

sources.citation: Odumuh, Adama Emmanuel. 1994. Profile of the language situation: Idoma. Paper, 25th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, Rutgers (ERIC ED375664), 47 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Its short sound-system section (alphabet, diacritics, tone; paper p.17-18 = PDF p.19) quotes Armstrong n.d. 'Idoma Orthography' p.13 verbatim: 'Idoma has a three tone-level discrete register tone system without downdrift or downstep except in the Southernmost dialect, Yala of Ikom, on the Cross River.. There are a great many sets of words which differ only by tone but which have quite different meanings.' followed by tonal minimal sets (ene, oko, ona).

sources.citation: Armstrong, Robert G. 1983. The Idomoid languages of the Benue and Cross River valleys. Journal of West African Languages 13(1): 91-149 (JWAL open scan, pp. 91-92 missing, no text layer; scanned at 200 dpi, one tesseract at a time).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing: full-text scanned of all 58 pages has no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent'. Typological remarks p.96-97: Igede has a four-level register tone system; 'All the other Idomoid languages have three-register systems. Except for the very special case of Yala (Ikom), downdrift is rare and downstep non-existent'; 'With very rare exceptions, all syllables are open'; section 3.1 gives consonant/vowel charts per Idoma dialect (Kyana, Idoma Nokwu, Agatu, Otukpo p.132, Agila, Yala) with vowel-harmony notes only; the appended Longley/Abraham comparison (p.126) treats tone only.

sources.citation: Armstrong, Robert G. 1968. Yala (Ikom), a terraced-level language with three tones. Journal of West African Languages 5(1): 49-58 (Yala Ikom lect = Yala [yba], not Central Idoma; scanned).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent: no 'stress'/'accent'). p.50: three contrastive tonal registers high/mid/low plus downstep; 'the other Idoma-Yala dialects so far studied have no downdrift and no terracing'; a Yala utterance can begin on any of the three tones, 'In this respect, Yala (Ikom) resembles all the other dialects of the Arago-Idoma-Yala Dialect Cluster.'

sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only full reference grammar of (Otukpo/Central) Idoma and the basis of all later work; Abraham marked three tones plus glides and, in his other grammars (Hausa, Tiv, Amharic), explicitly discussed stress vs. tone, so its phonology chapter is where a first-hand statement on Idoma stress/accent (or its absence) would be. Would supersede everything found here.
